rationale: B wins on grounding discipline. Its strongest angle, "Can a 1.8B model really match one 4x its size? Hugging Face's own numbers say maybe," keeps the benchmark claim in the only honest frame: testable, not proven. A has sharper range, especially "Hugging Face keeps the model free and starts charging for the plumbing around it," but it blows a hole in trust with "early customer for Hugging Face's offline AI model" when the update only says early enterprise customer. That is how a decent angle set walks into a correction.
gaps_in_A: "A Fortune 100 manufacturer just became an early customer for Hugging Face's offline AI model" invents or conflates a fact. The update says early enterprise customer, not customer for the offline model.
"a quiet challenge to the cloud-inference business every major AI lab depends on" overreaches. Offline capability supports the question; it does not prove a threat to API revenue.
"security-conscious buyers" and "data-residency" are plausible, but not supplied. They belong in proof-needed language, not as the premise.
The compliance-buyer and Fortune 100 customer angles may collapse into one unless the actual manufacturer use case supports both.
gaps_in_B: "privacy, cost, and latency case for local AI" imports benefits not stated in the update. Fine as reporting questions, too loose as stated rationale.
"regulated, conservative buyer" decorates the Fortune 100 manufacturer with traits the update does not establish.
"a platform known for free, open hosting" relies on outside context, not the supplied update. Not fatal, but it is still a grounding leak.
The next step should be `fact-check`, not `journalist-fit-check`; benchmark reproduction, customer name, license scope, and pricing terms need cleanup before journalist matching.
